title: Make a six-second demo

inspect.heading: Read the duration
inspect.intro: ffprobe reads a media file without changing it. Run the command with your source filename, then find the Duration line.
inspect.task: For the practice video, Duration: 00:00:12.00 means twelve seconds. Focus on that line; the course introduces the other fields later.
inspect.predict: Does this recording contain enough time for a six-second edit?
inspect.resultNote: This report comes from the ffprobe command you ran against the selected workspace file.
inspect.importResult: Find the duration in your file’s actual output. If the value is missing, do not treat it as zero; the course explains how to inspect recordings without a declared duration.
inspect.streamSummary: The practice recording has a twelve-second duration.
inspect.customResult: These are the results of your typed command. Read the output before continuing.

trim.heading: Keep the first six seconds
trim.intro: Start with one change: keep six seconds from the beginning. Predict what will remain, then run the command and replay the new file.
trim.task: -i names the source file; the final filename names the new output. -t 6 sets the output length to six seconds. Your source stays unchanged.
trim.importTask: Choose a length that fits inside your recording. Run the command and replay the new file to check which part you kept.
trim.predict: Change the duration from six seconds to four. Predict which end gets shorter, then use a new output filename to keep both versions and compare their replays.
trim.resultNote: FFmpeg produced this file. Replay it to check the action, result and any intended sound.
trim.review: Can a viewer follow the action and read its result? Check sound only if you intended it.
trim.exportUnavailable: Run an FFmpeg command successfully to create a downloadable output.
trim.tryAgain: Change the command and try again
trim.sourceSafe: Choose a different output filename to keep the source.
trim.startExperiment: After checking the first cut, set the start to two seconds and keep the duration at six. Use a new output filename so you can compare the two openings. Does starting later still give the action enough context?

flags.heading: What this command does
flags.input: -i names the source file. The final filename names a new output, so the source stays available.
flags.probeStreams: -show_streams reports each picture or sound stream.
flags.probeFormat: -show_format reports the container, which organises the streams and their timing.
flags.probeDefault: ffprobe FILE reads the file without editing it. Find Duration in its output; the practice video’s 00:00:12.00 means twelve seconds.
flags.probeJson: For a structured report, switch to Type command and add -show_streams -show_format -of json. You can also add -v error to hide routine log messages.
flags.start: -ss chooses the start time in seconds. Here it goes after -i and the input filename: FFmpeg reads the input and discards the part before that start. -t still sets how long the output lasts.
flags.duration: -t 6 keeps six seconds. It sets the output length; it does not name an end time in the source.
flags.mapVideo: -map 0:v:0 selects the first video stream from input 0.
flags.mapAudio: -map '0:a?' selects audio from input 0 when it exists. The question mark makes that selection optional.
flags.encode: -c:v libx264 encodes pictures as H.264. -c:a aac encodes sound as AAC.
flags.pixels: -pix_fmt yuv420p chooses a widely supported way to store picture colour.
